summary: Two topics: First, a brief discussion of leap year contract rules (dates extended for the later party's benefit), after which the Gemara returns to the Yom Kippur service. Second, the scapegoat service: the HP approaches the Azazel goat, places both hands on its head, and recites the third comprehensive confession. A designated guide then takes the goat to the wilderness while the HP returns to the Temple for the communal services. The guide acts as the HP's legal agent, completing the dispatch that the HP's confession and hand-laying initiated.

learning.ahaMoment: The HP's hands on the scapegoat's head: this moment bridges the inner service (blood in the Holy of Holies) and the outer service (scapegoat in the wilderness). The HP himself is the bridge - his hands connect the sanctuary to the wilderness.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two hands, one goat, all of Israel: the HP's body is the bridge between the most sacred space and the most desolate place.
learning.learnerQuestion: What is the HP's physical role in the Azazel service, and what does placing both hands on the goat's head accomplish?
learning.coreTension: The HP has already confessed twice - once for himself and once for the kohanim. Now he approaches the Azazel goat for a third confession. Why a third confession, and why both hands specifically?
learning.coreMove: The HP places both hands on the Azazel goat's head and recites a third comprehensive confession, this time transferring all Israel's sins collectively. This act bridges the inner Temple service (blood sprinklings) with the outer world (Azazel). He then hands the goat to the designated guide.

takeaway.text: The HP's third confession - both hands on the goat's head - is the moment of communal transfer: all Israel's sins are collectively placed on the scapegoat before it departs.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may conflate the three confessions. The first covered the HP himself, the second covered all kohanim - this third one covers all of Israel, and the physical hand-laying completes the transfer ritual.

learning.ahaMoment: The HP and the guide are two parts of one service: the HP provides the intentional act (confession, hand-laying), the guide provides the dispatch act. Neither alone constitutes the complete service.
learning.memoryAnchor: HP at the gate, guide on the road: a divided service with two essential actors completing one atonement.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why doesn't the HP accompany the Azazel goat to the cliff himself, and what is the guide's legal status in completing the service?
learning.coreTension: The HP began the Azazel service but cannot complete it - the guide takes over. Is this a practical division of labor, or does the guide have a distinct halachic role?
learning.coreMove: The HP needs to remain for subsequent Temple services. The guide acts as his legal agent (shaliach), completing the Azazel dispatch. The HP provides intention and conferral; the guide provides execution. Together they constitute one unified service.

takeaway.text: The guide is the HP's legal agent for the Azazel dispatch - not a mere helper but a halachic extension of the HP's service, whose acts are attributed to the HP.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may view the guide as merely logistical. The key is agency: the guide's acts are attributed to the HP. The service is not split between two independent actors but unified through the law of agency.

rashiTranslations.en: 'And if it was intercalated, it was intercalated for the seller' - meaning the house is not finalized in the buyer's possession until that same day
of that same month arrives in which he sold it to him; and according to Rabbi, you can find this applying, for instance, where he consecrated the animal on the eighth day
after its birth, on the eve of Yom Kippur in a plain year, and by the time the next Yom Kippur
arrives, only 364 days have passed for it, not 365. 'What can be said regarding the bull' -
since it is three years old. 'We view it' -
as though, wherever it is, it stands in
a cemetery, since the priest cannot come near it;
but it is not among the sin-offerings that must die,
only that it cannot be offered; therefore it grazes
until a blemish befalls it and it is sold. 'On account of
a mishap' - the Gemara will explain below what this mishap is.
'As we learned' - that we are concerned about a mishap. 'One may not consecrate' -
anything, since an unspecified consecration goes to Temple maintenance,
and there is no remedy for it. 'And one may not devote' -
he holds that an unspecified devotion goes to Temple maintenance,
and this is a matter of dispute in tractate Arachin (28b).
'All that graze' - all these cases where the Rabbis said
they should graze until they become blemished, we are concerned lest
one offer them. 'And those that are not themselves fit
for offering' - the other grazing animals do not themselves stand
to be offered, only their proceeds after sale. 'He is not
preoccupied with them' - he does not dwell on offering them,
and his mind is diverted from offering them.
'This one, which is fit for offering' - for the coming
Yom Kippur, his mind is preoccupied with offering it,
and he might offer it before Yom Kippur.
'It is a dispute among Tannaim' - there is one who is concerned and one who is not
concerned. 'It shall be offered on the second' - on Pesach Sheni, it shall be sold
to one who is impure or was on a distant journey. 'This is Rabbi's view' -
who says that from one Pesach to the next it is possible for its year not
to have passed, even though it was set aside after
the eighth day from its birth, since an animal lacking its time is not
consecrated. 'And likewise the money' - that was set aside for a Pesach-offering
should not be used to offer in the following year; but there is one
who says it may be used. 'Mishnah: he comes to'
'the goat' - now the Tanna returns to his subject
to instruct us in the order of the service, and he says that after
the High Priest finished placing the blood of the bull
and the goat, as concluded at the end of the chapter Hotzi'u Lo, comes
the priest to the goat that is sent away, at the place
where they had stationed it opposite the House of its Dispatch,
as we said in the chapter Teref BeKalfi (above, daf 41b).
'Except that the priests made it a fixed practice' - they became accustomed
to make it the priests' fixed practice to
lead it, and the court of
priests would not allow an Israelite to lead it.
'Arsela' - the name of the man. 'And a ramp' - they made for him a kind
of raised platform, high up, and he would go out
by way of that ramp, outside the courtyard and outside
the city, so that the Babylonians could not touch
the one being sent away, since they used to pull out his hair
and say to him, 'Take our sins and go quickly, and do not
delay our iniquities with us any longer.'
'Gemara' - the comment is completed on 66b as 'that it be ready,' explaining the word 'iti' from the braita cited here.
